newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgians demand change, but will it come?.
newsitem.headline: Belgians demand change, but will it come?.

text.p: Organisers asked for a strong, dignified showing and they got it when hundreds of thousands of Belgians swarmed into Brussels to demand radical changes to a judicial and political system seen as morally bankrupt.

The mass march to express support for the victims of a paedophile ring and demonstrate disgust at a system that allowed it to operate for so long has put the government under unprecedented pressure with suspicions of a high-level cover-up.

It could be a catalyst for change in a country that was shocked out of its usual phlegmatism by the discovery of the bodies of four girls killed by a paedophile gang and the rescue of two others who had been sexually abused.

But the process is likely to be accelerated evolution rather than revolution in a nation which has little self-image, less self confidence and where politicians spend a good portion of their time setting one half of the people against the other.

Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who privately met the parents of some of the dead, sexually abused and missing children, promised that changes would be made quickly and nothing would be allowed to hinder the investigations.
"This is a strong signal which we cannot ignore," Dehaene told reporters. "It is good that people encourage politicians. This movement will speed up (the reforms)."

This may satisfy some people for a while, but the mood sweeping Belgium indicates that political blandishments will not hold the tide for long. Changes will have to be made and, more importantly, be seen to be made.

"Our anger is growing now. For years we stayed silent and just nodded our heads, but now it is too much," mother-of-two Corin Delancker told Reuters at the start of Sunday's march by more than a quarter of a million people through Brussels.
"Justice must be for the people now. For everyone not just for the people with money or power," she said.

She was by no means alone, judging by the placards dotting the march calling for a rehumanisation of the law, for names of offenders to be revealed and for an end to the alleged protection of people in high places.

"I am in the street today because I want to shoulder my responsibilities instead of complaining and criticising ceaselessly for years without doing anything about what some of our politicians have been doing," said a statement handed out by a woman who simply signed herself "a Belgian citizen".
In an unusual and potentially constitutionally risky gambit, King Albert has added his voice to the chorus of calls for a clean out.

But change will not be easy in a legal and judicial system riddled from top to bottom with political patronage and with deep and enduring distrust between the French-speaking Walloon and Dutch-speaking Flemish populations.
The people called upon to institute the changes have themselves come up through the patronage system and are therefore deemed by the general public to be suspect.
A more independent, professional group of people may now be working their way up the ladder. But so many and varied are the pitfalls they face that their effect can only be cumulative.

It could be a positive omen that the linguistic divide was swept aside as Belgians from all walks of life expressed their revulsion at the almost daily revelations of child sex abuse and police and legal bungling and incompetence.
Whether this is strong enough to survive the inevitable setbacks still to come will be the true test of the nation.
